title: Why Product Management Will Never Give You Instant Gratification
author: Benedikt
summary: Benedikt of Leading in Product argues that the long silence after shipping is not a warning sign for a product manager but the nature of the job. Sales and marketing get fast scoreboards, whereas product impact can take eighteen months to appear and three years from idea to real traction. He gives two causes: products need time to mature, and there is no agreed definition of success across metrics such as DAU, revenue and retention. He adds that a generation raised on instant feedback feels the mismatch more sharply, while noting it spans all ages. His honest answer is that no framework or dashboard shortens the timeline, and tools claiming otherwise offer vanity metrics. The skill that separates lasting managers from those who burn out is operating with clarity and confidence while the scoreboard is blank. The piece is filed under Leadership as a reflection on leading oneself through delayed feedback.
points: Product work lacks the quick scoreboards of sales or marketing, and impact can take eighteen months or more to show.
Success has no single definition, so the scoreboard is a shifting set of signals that colleagues will interpret differently.
Fast-feedback habits from modern life create a real mismatch with the pace of product work, and it is not a character flaw.
No OKR framework or dashboard shortens the maturity curve, and tools that promise real-time proof deliver vanity metrics.
The durable skill is trusting well-founded thinking while data has not yet arrived.
quotes: Sales reps know their numbers at the end of every week. Marketers run a campaign and see results within days. A few weeks at most, three months at the absolute outer edge.

A feature you shipped six months ago might not show meaningful impact for another eighteen months. Users have to find it, try it, build habits around it - and only then does the data start to tell a coherent story.
You can hit your DAU target and still be building exactly the wrong thing. You can grow revenue while quietly losing your most valuable users.
An entire generation has entered the workforce already wired for fast, visible feedback. You post something and get a response within minutes.
No OKR framework changes the fundamental timeline of product work. No weekly metrics review fast-forwards the maturity curve.

Trusting your thinking during the long stretches where the data has simply not arrived yet. Not because you are blindly optimistic, but because you have done the work, you understand the problem, and you know that good products take time.
The PMs who genuinely make peace with it are the ones who build things that matter and stick around long enough to see them land.
